title: Vaccination and Sterilization: The Foundation of Cat Health
content:
This article is your critically important guide to the two main pillars of your pet's long and happy life.

## Vaccination Schedule: When, Against What, and Why You Can't Skip It
Vaccination is not an option; it is an obligation. Vaccinations build immunity against fatal or severe diseases, even if the cat does not go outside. Viruses can be brought home on clothing and shoes.

*Panleukopenia (Feline Distemper/Highly Contagious, deadly)* Vaccinate:  Kittens: from 8–9 weeks (twice, with revaccination after 3–4 weeks). Adults: annually.
*Rhinotracheitis and Calicivirus(Components of "feline flu". Difficult to treat, affect the respiratory system.)* Vaccinate: Schedule similar to panleukopenia.
*Rabies(Deadly for cats and humans, mandatory by law in many regions.)* Vaccinate: Kittens: from 12 weeks. Adults: annually.
*Chlamydia, Leukemia(Vaccinated as indicated (contact with other animals, free-roaming))* Vaccinate: Discussed with a veterinarian individually.

**Conclusion:** NEVER skip the annual booster. A single vaccination in kittenhood is not enough to maintain immunity.

title: Optimal Age for Spaying/Neutering
content:
Spaying (removal of ovaries and uterus in females) and neutering (removal of testicles in males) are the most common planned surgeries.

*Optimal Age:* 6–8 months.

## Arguments "FOR" Early Procedure:
*Cancer prevention:* Spaying before the first heat cycle reduces the risk of mammary cancer almost to zero.
*Behavioral issues:* Prevents urine marking in male cats and loud "singing" during heat in female cats.
*Uterine health:* Completely eliminates pyometra (pus infection of the uterus) — a life-threatening condition in unspayed cats.

## Debatable Points:
*"Early" neutering (4–6 months). Studies:* It is safe. It does not affect growth, development, or the risk of obesity any more than neutering at 8 months. It provides better behavioral outcomes.
*Risk of obesity. Studies:* Weight gain is linked not to the surgery, but to a change in metabolism and improper nutrition after the procedure. *Solution:* switch to sterilized cat food and control portions.
*"Let her have one litter for health". Studies:* This is a myth. Pregnancy and birth offer no health benefit to the cat and only increase the risk of complications.

**Conclusion:** Plan spaying/neutering for the optimal age of 6–8 months. Discuss pre-surgical screening (blood tests) with your vet to minimize risks. This is the most effective investment in your pet's health and tranquility.

title: Emergency Aid: Poisoning
content:
Every minute counts in a critical situation. Don't panic; follow this plan.

## Poisoning: List of Strictly Forbidden Substances
If you suspect poisoning, call your veterinarian immediately. Do not attempt to treat the cat yourself unless instructed by a doctor.

*Strictly forbidden for cats (deadly danger):*
*Human medications (NSAIDs):* Paracetamol (acetaminophen), Ibuprofen. One tablet of paracetamol causes liver necrosis and death!
*Plants:* Lilies, daylilies (all parts of the plant, even vase water, are deadly dangerous to the kidneys). Azalea, cyclamen, tulips.
*Foods/Ingredients:* Onions and garlic (in any form, cause anemia), Xylitol (sugar substitute).
*Household chemicals:* Antifreeze, cleaning agents, insecticides (especially organophosphates).

## What to do if you suspect poisoning:
Call the veterinary clinic immediately. Report what the cat ate, how much time has passed, and its condition. Follow the doctor's instructions.
*Do not induce vomiting yourself!* Some poisons (e.g., caustic substances) can cause an even greater burn to the esophagus upon return.
If the poison is on the fur/paws (e.g., household chemicals), put on a protective collar and rinse the area with clean water to prevent the cat from licking the poison.
If possible, take the packaging of the ingested substance or plant to the clinic with you.

**Conclusion:** In an emergency, the most important thing is to first call the veterinarian for clear instructions, and then ensure the fastest and safest delivery of your pet to the clinic.

title: Emergency Aid: Falls from Heights
content:
Every minute counts in a critical situation. Don't panic; follow this plan.

## Fall from Height (High-Rise Syndrome)
Don't assume a cat always lands on its feet. Falls from great heights (especially 5th–9th floor) often lead to severe injuries.

## What to do:
Examine the cat, but do not shake or move it unnecessarily. Any injuries, especially to the back or pelvis, require the most careful transportation.
Carefully place the cat on a hard, flat surface (board, plywood, thick cardboard) and secure it so it cannot move during transport.
*Rush to the clinic!* The most common and dangerous injuries:
*Lung rupture* or pneumothorax (air in the chest cavity).
*Bladder rupture.*
*Fractures of the jaw, limbs, and pelvis.*

**Conclusion:** In an emergency, the most important thing is to first call the veterinarian for clear instructions, and then ensure the fastest and safest delivery of your pet to the clinic.

title: Emergency Aid: Heatstroke
content:
Every minute counts in a critical situation. Don't panic; follow this plan.

## Heatstroke
Heatstroke most often occurs in closed, unventilated spaces or in a carrier during hot weather.

## Critical Signs:
*Rapid, heavy breathing* (panting) with an open mouth.
*Drooling* (foaming at the mouth).
*Gums are bright red* or, conversely, bluish.
*Lethargy, disorientation, vomiting.*

## Immediate Aid (can save a life):
Immediately move the cat to a cool, well-ventilated area.
*Cooling:* Soak a towel in cool (not icy!) water and wrap the cat, paying special attention to the armpits, groin, and abdomen. *Do not use ice* — it will cause blood vessel spasm.
*Water:* Offer water to drink, but do not force it.
Rush the cat to the veterinarian, continuing to cool it en route. Even if it seems better, internal organ damage must be ruled out.

**Conclusion:** In an emergency, the most important thing is to first call the veterinarian for clear instructions, and then ensure the fastest and safest delivery of your pet to the clinic.

title: Feeding: How Not to Harm and Choose the Best
content:
Diet is the basis of health. Improper nutrition can lead to obesity, urinary stones, and other serious problems.

## What is Allowed and What is Strictly Forbidden
Cats are obligate (strict) carnivores. Their bodies are adapted to digest animal proteins and fats.

*Foods that are strictly forbidden for cats:*
*Onions and garlic (in any form):* Contain sulfoxides that destroy red blood cells and cause anemia. Dangerous even in small amounts.
*Chocolate:* Contains theobromine — a toxin that cats cannot metabolize quickly.
*Alcohol and caffeine:* Can cause intoxication, tremors, and death.
*Raw dough, grapes, and raisins:* Can be toxic or cause dangerous bloating.
*Bones (especially tubular):* Can damage the esophagus, stomach, or intestines. Seriously dangerous!
*Raw freshwater fish:* Contains the enzyme thiaminase, which destroys Vitamin B1, leading to neurological problems.

*Caution (better to avoid or strictly control):*
*Milk:* Most adult cats have lactose intolerance, causing diarrhea and digestive upset.
*Raw fish/meat:* Carries the risk of parasites and bacteria (Salmonella). If given, the product must be frozen and comply with veterinary and sanitary standards.

## The Debate on Food: Dry vs. Wet vs. Raw Diet
Owners often debate which type of food is better. It is important to understand that quality and balance are key.

*Commercial Foods (Dry/Wet)*
*Pros:* Completely balanced with vitamins and minerals (especially taurine). Saves time; dry food helps clean teeth.
*Cons and risks:* Risk of urinary stones (with dry food due to lack of moisture). Low-quality foods contain a lot of grain.

*Raw Diet (BARF/Raw)*
*Pros:* Complete control over ingredients. High animal protein content.
*Cons and risks:* Very high risk of imbalance (lack of calcium, taurine, vitamins). Requires consultation with a veterinary nutritionist and constant monitoring.

## How to Choose the Food Class
Choose commercial food based on its composition, not its price.
*Holistic:* Ideal choice. Contains the maximum possible amount of meat (first ingredients listed), often grain-free and without artificial additives.
*Super Premium:* A very good choice. Meat is listed first, well-digestible, and balanced.
*Premium:* Satisfactory. May contain more grains and by-products.
*Economy (Whiskas, Kitekat, etc.):* Not recommended. Based on cereals, low meat content, poorly digestible, often leads to health problems.

**Conclusion:** By choosing high-quality commercial food (holistic or super-premium), you provide your cat with all necessary nutrients. A combination of dry and wet food is often considered optimal, as wet food compensates for lack of fluids and serves as prevention against kidney and urinary tract problems.

title: Litter Box and Litter Types
content:
Toilet problems are a common cause of stress for both the cat and the owner. The right choice and adherence to simple rules will minimize them.

## How to Choose a Litter Box: Size, Type, and Quantity
The most common mistake is a litter box that is too small.
*Size matters:* The litter box should be one and a half times the length of your cat (from nose tip to tail base). The cat must be able to turn around and dig freely in it.

*Litter Box Type:*
*Open:* Best. Cats feel safer in it and have escape routes if something scares them.
*Closed (hooded):* May be convenient for the owner (less odor and litter around), but the cat may dislike it due to stale odor or a confined feeling.

*The N+1 Rule:* There should be one more litter box in the house than the number of cats. For example, if you have one cat, you need two litter boxes. Place them in different, easily accessible locations.
*Where not to place:* The litter box should not be placed next to food and water bowls, or in very noisy areas (near a washing machine) or busy corridors.

## Overview of Litter Types: Pros and Cons
The cat chooses litter based on feel (texture) and smell. Choose based on their preference and your ability to clean.

*Bentonite (Clay) Clumping*
*Pros:* Clumps excellently, holds odor well. Resembles sand, which cats love to dig.
*Cons:* Can be dusty. Cannot be flushed down the toilet.

*Silica Gel*
*Pros:* Absorbs odor and moisture excellently. Infrequent replacement (about once a month).
*Cons:* Crunches loudly, which may frighten timid cats. High price.

*Wood/Pellet*
*Pros:* Environmentally friendly, can be flushed down the toilet. Inexpensive.
*Cons:* Quickly breaks down into sawdust after getting wet, may not hold odor well, tracks around the house.

*Important Tip:* If your cat suddenly starts eliminating outside the box, first rule out a medical cause (cystitis, urinary stones, pain) and only then look for a behavioral cause.

**Conclusion:** Provide a litter box of the right size, always keep it clean, and use the litter your cat likes. Cleanliness is key to good behavior!

title: Scratching Post and Claws
content:
Scratching is not naughtiness but a vital need for the cat. It sharpens its claws to mark territory, remove the old claw layer, and stretch its muscles. Your task is to redirect this instinct.

## How to Train Your Cat to Use a Scratching Post
*Never punish* your cat for scratching furniture. Punishment will only cause fear of you but will not eliminate the instinct.
*Correct placement:* Put the scratching post where the cat is already scratching (near the sofa or armchair), or where it often sleeps and stretches (at the exit of a room).
*Size and material:* The scratching post should be tall (the cat should be able to stretch out to its full length) and stable. Popular materials: *sisal* (more durable) or *cardboard* (many cats adore it).
*Horizontal or vertical?* Offer both options. Some cats prefer to scratch on a horizontal surface (a flat cardboard scratcher), others on a vertical one (a post).
*Stimulation:* Sprinkle catnip on the scratching post or attach a favorite toy to it to create a positive association.
*Furniture protection:* Temporarily cover favorite scratching spots with thick fabric or double-sided tape (cats dislike stickiness) during training.

## How to Trim Claws Correctly
Trimming claws is simple and necessary to prevent ingrown claws and preserve furniture.
*Tool:* Use special cat nail clippers (guillotine or scissor type).
*Technique:* Gently press on the paw pad to fully extend the claw. Cut only the white, transparent tip of the claw.
*Critical zone:* Inside the claw is the pink part (the quick), where nerve endings and blood vessels run. This must not be cut! With dark-colored claws, this boundary is harder to see, so only trim the very tip.
*What to do if you cut the quick?* It is painful and will bleed. Don't panic! Immediately apply styptic powder, cornstarch, or flour to the wound and hold pressure. Do not scold the cat.
*Frequency:* Trim claws every 2–4 weeks. Start training the kitten for the procedure with simple paw massage and praise.

**Conclusion:** The scratching post must be more appealing than the sofa. Claw trimming should become a routine, calm procedure that your cat associates only with praise.

title: Frequent Disputes: Outdoor Access
content:
Cat owners often encounter conflicting information. Here's what veterinarians and felinologists say about the most popular discussions.

## Does an indoor cat need outdoor access?
*Answer:* Absolutely not, unless you can ensure complete safety.

*Opinion: "They need to go out"*
*Argument:* The cat is bored; it needs to "feel nature."
*Critical Note:* Outside, the cat faces: *parasites* (fleas, worms), *dangerous infections* (panleukopenia, rabies, leukemia virus), cars, mean people, and other animals.

*Opinion: "It should stay indoors"*
*Argument:* Safety and longevity.
*Critical Note:* Indoor cats live longer and healthier lives. All their needs (physical activity, hunting, observing nature) can be fully met indoors (climbing structures, "cat TV" by the window, interactive games).

**Conclusion:** If you do not live in a completely isolated private house, free-roaming for a cat is a death lottery. It is better to teach it to walk on a harness under your supervision in a safe place or install protection on windows ("cat-proof screens").

title: Frequent Disputes: Sleeping in Bed
content:
Should a cat sleep in the owner's bed: Myths and Reality

*Answer:* It is safe with proper hygiene.

*Question: Is it dangerous for health?*
*What you need to know:* The risk is minimal if you regularly deworm and treat for fleas. The most common parasites people can catch from cats (toxoplasmosis, worms) are transmitted through feces, not through fur.

*Question: Does it affect sleep?*
*What you need to know:* Cats are nocturnal animals; their activity cycle can disrupt your sleep. If the cat interferes, it is better to designate a cozy spot near the bed for it.

*Question: Does it affect behavior?*
*What you need to know:* It is a myth that co-sleeping spoils the character. The cat does not consider itself the "boss" because it sleeps with you. It is simply a sign of trust and attachment.

**Conclusion:** If you are comfortable, and you regularly perform anti-parasitic treatment, co-sleeping with your cat is a wonderful way to strengthen your bond.

title: Frequent Disputes: Cats shouldn't be given dry food non-stop
content:
*Answer:* They can, if it's quality food and they have access to water.

Many argue that a cat needs constantly changing food. In fact, a cat's stomach is very conservative.

*What is good:* High-quality, balanced dry food (super-premium/holistic) that suits your cat can be its constant diet for life.

*What is bad:* Frequent changes in food can, conversely, cause digestive upset and stress.

*The main rule:* If feeding only dry food, the cat must drink plenty of water. Provide it with access to clean water in several places or purchase a drinking fountain.
